seed.q: In a min-heap holding many values, where does the smallest value sit?
opts: In a leaf, because small values sink
In the last slot of the backing array
At the root, above every other value
Wherever it was inserted, since heaps only reorder on demand
seed.e: Every node in a min-heap is at least as large as its parent, so from any node you can walk upward through non-increasing values until you reach the root, which makes the root the minimum. A heap of 1048576 shuffled values held 1 at index 0, and through 1000 mixed pushes and pops index 0 kept holding the smallest value still in the heap. Leaves hold the large values, the backing array is not sorted so its last slot means nothing, and the sift-up on every insert is exactly the reordering that a heap is claimed not to do.
seed.intro: The heap rule compares each node only with its parent. Follow that comparison upward from any node and see where you end up.

seed.q: What is the time complexity of finding (peeking at) the minimum in a min-heap?
seed.e: The heap-order property pins the minimum at index 0, so peeking is a single array read whose cost does not grow with n: on heaps of 16 and of 1048576 elements the peek was one access either way. O(log n) is the cost of extract-min, which removes the root and then sifts a replacement down the full height - confusing peeking with extracting is the usual mistake. O(n) would mean scanning the array, which the invariant makes unnecessary.
seed.intro: Peeking does not change the heap. Recall which position the heap-order property pins the minimum to.

seed.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting one element into a binary heap of n elements?
seed.e: An insert appends at the end of the array and sifts the value up one parent at a time, so the number of swaps is bounded by the height, about log2 n: on a heap of 1048575 elements the deepest sift-up took 19 swaps, matching floor(log2 n). Average behavior is far cheaper - inserting the same values in random order needed about 1.3 swaps per insert - which is why O(1) is the average-case answer rather than a nonsense one, and why the stem has to say which case it means. O(n) would mean touching the whole array, which a sift-up never does.
seed.intro: A new value enters at the bottom and can only move upward along one path. How long can that path be?

seed.q: Removing the minimum (extract-min) from a binary heap of n elements costs, in the worst case:
seed.e: Extract-min removes the root, moves the last element into its place and sifts it down one level at a time, so the work is bounded by the height. Over 200000 extractions from a 1048575-element heap the deepest sift-down was 19 swaps, exactly floor(log2 n), and the average was 18.6 - unlike insertion, this operation is logarithmic on average as well as in the worst case. O(1) is what peeking at the minimum costs when you do not remove it, which is the usual confusion.
seed.intro: The root is gone, so a value from the bottom takes its place and has to settle. Count the levels it can fall through.

seed.q: A binary heap is most commonly implemented using:
opts: A binary tree of linked nodes
An array indexed level by level
A hash map from index to value
A linked list in level order
seed.e: Because a binary heap is complete, laying it out in level order leaves no holes, so with 0-based indices the children of position i are always at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent at floor((i-1)/2); a 1048576-element heap built on exactly that arithmetic stayed valid throughout. A 1-based array uses 2i and 2i+1 instead, which is why the convention has to be stated. Linked nodes or a hash map would also work, but each step then costs a pointer chase or a hash lookup and gives up the contiguous layout that makes the index arithmetic free.
seed.intro: A binary heap is always a complete tree, with no gaps on any level but the last. What does that let you compute instead of store?

seed.q: A priority queue must repeatedly insert values and remove the highest-priority one. Which structure keeps both operations efficient as n grows?
seed.e: A heap keeps both insert and remove-min at O(log n) because each one walks a single root-to-leaf path: pushing and then draining 100000 values cost about 30 operations per element. An unsorted array makes insert trivial but pays for it on every removal, which has to scan for the minimum - the same workload cost about 50000 operations per element - and keeping a list sorted just moves that linear cost into the insert. A hash table has no ordering at all, so it cannot find the highest-priority entry without a full scan.
seed.intro: Two operations have to stay cheap at the same time. Ask which structure avoids scanning everything on the removal.

seed.q: Building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements (heapify) can be done in:
seed.e: Bottom-up heapify sifts each element down at most its own height, and almost all elements sit near the bottom: half are leaves that move zero levels, a quarter move at most one, and the total stays proportional to n. Measured, building heaps of 1023 and of 1048575 elements took about 0.7 swaps per element at both sizes - a constant, not a growing one. O(n log n) is what you get by inserting the n elements one at a time, which cost 18.0 swaps per element on the worst-case input at the same size.
seed.intro: Half the elements are leaves and need no work at all. Ask how far the typical element actually has to sift.

seed.q: Heap sort works by building a heap and repeatedly extracting the root; its overall time complexity is:
seed.e: The build phase is linear, but each of the n extract-min operations sifts a replacement down about log2 n levels, so the removals dominate and the total is n log n. Counted comparisons stayed between 1.69 and 1.84 times n times log2 n as n grew from 1024 to 1048576 - a bounded constant, not a growing one. O(n) is the cost of the build phase alone, the tempting mistake immediately after learning that heapify is linear, and O(n squared) would require each removal to scan the whole array, which sifting down never does.
seed.intro: Building the heap is the cheap half. Count what the n removals cost, since each one has to restore the heap.

opts: Vertices that must all be connected
A single root and its descendants
Vertices and the edges connecting them
A square matrix of connection flags
seed.e: A graph is a set of vertices together with a set of edges, each edge joining a pair of vertices; both parts are part of the definition. Connectivity is not required, so a graph may fall into several disconnected pieces, and a rooted tree is only the special case with no cycles and one designated root. A square matrix of flags is one way to store a graph - the adjacency matrix - not what a graph is.
seed.intro: Ask what a graph could still express if you took away the connections and kept only the objects.

seed.q: In a directed graph, an edge:
opts: may be followed from either endpoint
always comes with a matching reverse edge
runs one way, from a source to a target
carries a weight in addition to a direction
seed.e: A directed edge is an ordered pair: it runs from a source vertex to a target, and its existence says nothing about whether the reverse edge exists. That asymmetry is the point - you may not follow it backward unless the reverse edge is separately present, which is why reachability in a directed graph has to be computed rather than assumed. Weights are a separate, optional attribute; a directed edge does not need one.
seed.intro: An undirected edge is an unordered pair of endpoints. Ask what changes once that pair becomes ordered.

seed.q: Using adjacency lists, what is the time complexity of breadth-first search over a graph with V vertices and E edges?
seed.e: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued once and each adjacency-list entry is read once, so the total is proportional to V plus E: on a graph with V = 64000 and E = 69232 the traversal made exactly 64000 vertex visits and 138464 edge inspections, which is 2E because an undirected edge appears in both endpoints' lists. O(V) ignores the edge scanning and O(E) ignores isolated vertices, so neither bound covers both halves of the work. The representation is what makes this bound true - the same BFS over an adjacency matrix inspected V squared, or 4096000000, cells on that graph.
seed.intro: Half the graph could be vertices that no edge touches, while one vertex could have a thousand neighbors. A bound has to survive both.

seed.q: Using adjacency lists, what is the time complexity of depth-first search over a graph with V vertices and E edges?
seed.e: DFS marks each vertex once and reads each adjacency-list entry once, so it does the same V plus E work that BFS does and only the visit order differs: on a graph with V = 64000 and E = 69232, both traversals made 64000 vertex visits and 138464 edge inspections. O(V squared) is not a random wrong answer - it is what DFS costs on an adjacency matrix, where finding a vertex's neighbors means scanning a whole row of V cells, which came to 4096000000 inspections on that same graph. That is why the stem has to say which representation it assumes.
seed.intro: Ask whether the walk can read the same neighbor list a second time, and what stops it.

seed.q: Which data structure does BFS use to manage which vertex to visit next?
seed.e: A queue is first-in-first-out, so vertices leave it in the order they were discovered and BFS finishes every vertex at distance k before any at distance k+1. Take a source with three neighbors, one of which starts a chain of three more: the queue-driven walk visits them at distances 0,1,1,1,2,3,4, while swapping in a stack sends the same code down the chain first, at distances 0,1,2,3,4,1,1 - a depth-first walk, so the shortest-path distances BFS is used for come out wrong. A heap would order by priority rather than by discovery, which gives Dijkstra, not BFS.
seed.intro: BFS is usually run to get the number of steps from the source. Ask which container would let a far vertex come out before a near one.

seed.q: An adjacency matrix representation of a graph with V vertices uses how much space?
seed.e: An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for every ordered pair of vertices, so the space is V times V no matter how many edges exist: at V = 64000 that is 4096000000 cells, while the same sparse graph's adjacency lists held 138464 entries. O(V + E) is the adjacency-list cost and O(E) counts only the edges that are present - the matrix pays for the absent ones too. It earns that space back only on dense graphs, where E approaches V squared, and by answering is there an edge from a to b in constant time.
seed.intro: Work out the cost for a graph with no edges at all, then for one with every possible edge. Compare the two.

seed.q: Dijkstra’s algorithm is used to find:
opts: the cheapest set of edges connecting every vertex
shortest paths from one source, given non-negative weights
an ordering of vertices that respects every dependency
the groups of vertices that can all reach each other
seed.e: Dijkstra grows a set of settled vertices outward from a single source, always finishing the nearest unsettled vertex, which yields the shortest distance from that source to every other vertex. The method holds only while no edge weight is negative: on a four-vertex graph with one weight of -3 it reported a distance of 5 where the true shortest path costs 3, because it had already settled that vertex and never reconsidered it. A minimum spanning tree is a different object - the cheapest edge set that connects everything, which need not contain any shortest path - while topological order and strongly connected components ignore weights entirely.
seed.intro: Cheapest route from one chosen vertex and cheapest set of edges overall are different results. Two of these options are exactly that pair.

seed.q: A topological sort can be performed on which kind of graph?
opts: An undirected graph with no cycles
A directed graph with no cycles
seed.e: A topological order lists the vertices so that every edge points forward, which needs direction - an undirected edge gives no meaning to before - and forbids cycles, since a cycle would require each of its vertices to come before itself. Running Kahn's algorithm on a five-vertex directed acyclic graph (a DAG) emitted all five in order; on a graph containing the cycle 0 to 1 to 2 to 0 it emitted none of the four, because no vertex ever reaches in-degree zero. Treating undirected edges as edges in both directions makes every edge a two-cycle, so that case fails for exactly the same reason.
seed.intro: Try to write a valid order for three tasks where each one waits on the next, in a loop. Where you get stuck is half the answer.
